short: Leucine is an essential amino acid that acts as a key trigger for muscle protein synthesis, which is why protein powders are often compared by their leucine content.
body: Leucine is one of the nine essential amino acids, meaning your body cannot make it and you have to get it from food. It is also one of the three branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs), along with isoleucine and valine. Beyond being a building block of protein, leucine works as a signal: when blood leucine rises after a meal, it helps switch on the cell machinery (the mTORC1 pathway) that starts building new muscle protein.

Because of that signaling role, researchers talk about a leucine "threshold" per meal. The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand on protein says a single protein dose should aim for about 700 to 3,000 mg (0.7 to 3 g) of leucine, alongside a balanced mix of the other essential amino acids. For most adults that lines up with 20 to 40 g of a high-quality protein, or about 0.25 g of protein per kg of body weight per meal.

Leucine content varies a lot by protein source. Dairy proteins such as whey are among the richest, at roughly 10 to 11% leucine by weight, so a 25 g serving of whey protein supplies around 2.5 to 3 g. Most plant proteins contain less per gram, which is one reason plant blends often use larger servings to reach the same leucine total. Collagen is very low in leucine.

Leucine is not the whole story. Studies of leucine or BCAAs taken alone show they cannot build muscle without the other essential amino acids, which serve as the raw materials. Think of leucine as the on switch and the rest of the essential amino acids as the bricks. Total daily protein intake still matters more than hitting an exact leucine number at every meal.
onLabel: Leucine usually appears in an optional amino acid profile table, listed in milligrams or grams per serving. If a brand lists only BCAAs, leucine is typically about half of that total in a 2:1:1 ratio.

short: BCAAs are three essential amino acids, leucine, isoleucine and valine, named for their branched chemical structure and sold both inside protein powders and as standalone supplements.
body: Branched-chain amino acids, or BCAAs, are leucine, isoleucine and valine. All three are essential amino acids, so they must come from your diet. Their name comes from the side chain on each molecule, which branches off like a fork. Unlike most amino acids, BCAAs are broken down largely in muscle rather than the liver, which made them an early focus of sports nutrition research.

Every complete protein already contains BCAAs. A typical 25 g serving of whey protein provides roughly 5 to 6 g of BCAAs, and plant proteins contain somewhat less. Standalone BCAA products usually supply 5 to 10 g per scoop, most often in a 2:1:1 ratio of leucine to isoleucine to valine.

The research on BCAA supplements by themselves is not encouraging for muscle building. A 2017 review by Robert Wolfe in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition concluded that BCAAs alone do not promote muscle anabolism. Building new muscle protein requires all nine essential amino acids. If you only supply three, the body has to break down existing protein to get the other six, which limits any net gain. A full protein or an essential amino acid (EAA) blend gives you the BCAAs plus the rest.

Some people still use BCAA drinks during training for taste or as a low-calorie flavored drink, and a few studies report less muscle soreness, though results are mixed. If you already eat enough total protein, extra BCAAs are unlikely to add much. For a protein powder, the BCAA number is mostly useful as a rough quality check: an unusually low figure for the stated protein can hint at a lower-quality or spiked formula.
onLabel: Brands often print a BCAA total per serving on the front of the tub or in an amino acid table. Standalone BCAA products list leucine, isoleucine and valine separately in a Supplement Facts panel.

short: Essential amino acids are the nine amino acids your body cannot make on its own, so they must come from food or supplements to build and repair protein.
body: Proteins are made from 20 amino acids. Your body can make 11 of them, but nine must come from your diet. These nine essential amino acids (EAAs) are histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. A protein that supplies all nine in useful amounts is often called a complete protein.

EAAs are what actually drive muscle protein synthesis. According to the ISSN position stands on protein and on nutrient timing, about 10 g of essential amino acids can maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis in many people, and doses from about 6 to 15 g all have a stimulating effect. A 20 to 40 g serving of a high-quality protein such as whey, milk, egg or soy delivers roughly that amount.

The balance of EAAs is what protein quality scores measure. Scores such as PDCAAS and DIAAS compare a protein's EAA profile to human needs and adjust for how well it is digested. The EAA in shortest supply is called the limiting amino acid. In pea protein it is usually methionine, in rice protein it is lysine, and collagen lacks tryptophan entirely.

Standalone EAA supplements are also sold, typically 5 to 15 g per scoop. They may be useful if you want a low-calorie amino acid drink, but for most people a complete protein serving provides the same EAAs plus other nutrients, usually at a lower cost per gram. Getting enough total protein from varied sources covers EAA needs for most healthy adults.
onLabel: Some labels include an amino acid profile listing each EAA in milligrams per serving. A front-label claim such as "10 g EAAs" is a marketing total, so check the table behind it.

short: PDCAAS is a protein quality score from 0 to 1.0 that compares a protein's essential amino acids to human needs and adjusts for how well it is digested.
body: The Protein Digestibility-Corrected Amino Acid Score, or PDCAAS, rates how well a protein meets human essential amino acid needs. It was adopted by FAO and WHO in 1991 and is still the method the U.S. FDA uses for protein labeling. A score of 1.0 is the top value. A score of 0.5 means the protein covers roughly half of your need for its scarcest essential amino acid.

The calculation has two steps. First, the protein's amino acid profile is compared to a reference pattern, and the lowest ratio (the limiting amino acid) becomes the amino acid score. Second, that score is multiplied by the protein's fecal digestibility, meaning how much protein disappears before it is excreted. Any result above 1.0 is cut down, or truncated, to 1.0.

Whey, casein, milk protein, egg white and soy protein isolate all score at or near 1.0. Pea protein usually scores somewhat lower, rice and hemp lower still, and collagen scores 0 because it lacks tryptophan. Plant blends such as pea plus rice can score higher than either one alone because each fills the other's gap.

PDCAAS has known weaknesses. Truncation hides real differences between high-quality proteins, so whey and soy look identical even though their profiles differ. Measuring digestibility at the end of the gut rather than the end of the small intestine can overestimate quality, because gut bacteria break down some protein that you never absorbed. For these reasons, the FAO recommended in 2013 that DIAAS replace PDCAAS, though PDCAAS remains in U.S. labeling rules.
onLabel: Under 21 CFR 101.9, the percent Daily Value for protein is calculated from PDCAAS-corrected protein. It is required when a product makes a protein claim, so a low %DV next to a high gram count can signal a lower-quality protein.

short: DIAAS is a protein quality score recommended by the FAO in 2013 that rates each essential amino acid by how much is absorbed in the small intestine.
body: The Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score, or DIAAS, is the newer way to judge protein quality. An FAO expert consultation recommended it in 2013 as a replacement for PDCAAS. "Indispensable" is another word for essential, so the score asks how well a protein supplies the nine essential amino acids your body must get from food.

DIAAS fixes two main problems with PDCAAS. First, it uses ileal digestibility, measured at the end of the small intestine, where amino acids are actually absorbed. Second, it looks at the digestibility of each essential amino acid separately rather than using one figure for the whole protein. The lowest digestible amino acid ratio, expressed as a percentage, becomes the score.

DIAAS values for single foods are not capped at 100, so higher-quality proteins can be told apart. The FAO report suggested cut-offs: 100 or more for an "excellent" or "high" quality claim, 75 to 99 for a "good" source, and below 75 for no quality claim. In a 2017 pig study in the British Journal of Nutrition, whey and milk protein concentrates scored 100 or more, soy protein isolate landed in the 75 to 99 range, and pea protein concentrate scored below 75. The same study found the older PDCAAS method tended to overrate lower-quality proteins.

DIAAS is harder and costlier to measure, and most values come from pig studies or small human trials, so published numbers vary by method, processing and the reference age group used. It is not used on U.S. labels. Treat any brand's DIAAS claim as useful but check which age reference and data source it relies on.
onLabel: DIAAS does not appear on the U.S. Nutrition Facts panel. When it shows up, it is a brand marketing claim, so look for the cited study or reference pattern.

short: Whey protein concentrate is a filtered form of whey, the liquid left after cheesemaking, that contains about 25 to 89% protein, most commonly about 80% in powders.
body: Whey is the watery part of milk that separates from the curds when cheese is made. Whey protein concentrate (WPC) is produced by filtering that liquid to remove much of the water, lactose and minerals, then drying it into powder. The protein level can range from about 25% to 89%. The version used in most protein powders is WPC80, which is roughly 80% protein by weight.

Compared with whey isolate, concentrate keeps more of the milk's fat and lactose. A typical WPC80 serving has a few grams of carbohydrate and fat. That gives it a creamier taste and usually a lower price per gram of protein. It also keeps more of the minor whey components, such as immunoglobulins and lactoferrin, though their health effects at the levels in a protein shake are not well established.

Nutritionally, WPC is a high-quality protein. It is rich in leucine, digests quickly and scores at the top of both PDCAAS and DIAAS. In a 2017 pig study in the British Journal of Nutrition, whey protein concentrate had a DIAAS above 100. Research on whey for muscle gain, including many studies in the ISSN position stand on protein, uses both concentrate and isolate.

The main reason to choose isolate instead is lactose. If you are sensitive to lactose, the extra lactose in concentrate may cause bloating or gas, while many people tolerate isolate better. If lactose is not an issue for you, concentrate is often the better value. Many products blend concentrate with isolate, so check the order of the ingredient list.
onLabel: Listed in the ingredients as "whey protein concentrate" or "WPC." Because ingredients are listed by weight, a product that names concentrate first contains more of it than any other ingredient.

short: Whey protein isolate is whey that has been filtered further than concentrate, reaching at least 90% protein by weight, with very little lactose or fat remaining.
body: Whey protein isolate (WPI) starts as the same liquid whey left over from cheesemaking. It is processed further than concentrate to strip out more fat and lactose. The usual industry standard is at least 90% protein on a dry-weight basis. A typical 30 g scoop of unflavored isolate provides about 25 to 27 g of protein, under 1 g of fat and usually under 1 g of lactose.

Two main methods are used. Microfiltration pushes whey through fine membranes that separate protein from fat and lactose. Ion exchange separates proteins by their electrical charge using pH changes. Both produce a high-protein powder. Some brands claim one method preserves more native protein fractions, but the evidence that this matters for muscle building is limited, since your stomach acid unfolds protein anyway.

WPI is one of the best-studied proteins in sports nutrition. The ISSN position stand on protein notes that whey isolates and hydrolysates are the most researched proteins for use around resistance training. Whey is digested quickly and is rich in leucine, with about 2.5 to 3 g per 25 g of protein. Whey isolate scores at the top of protein quality measures such as DIAAS.

Isolate costs more than concentrate per gram of protein. The main reasons to choose it are lower lactose, fewer calories from fat and carbohydrates, and a higher protein density per scoop. It also mixes thinner, which some people prefer. If you tolerate dairy well, concentrate delivers very similar muscle-building results for less money.
onLabel: Listed as "whey protein isolate" in the ingredients. Products called "100% isolate" should list no whey concentrate; if both appear, the one named first makes up more of the blend.

short: Whey protein hydrolysate is whey protein that has been partly broken down into smaller peptides using enzymes, so it is often described as pre-digested.
body: Whey protein hydrolysate (WPH) is made by treating whey concentrate or isolate with enzymes, or sometimes acid, that cut long protein chains into shorter pieces called peptides. The extent of this cutting is called the degree of hydrolysis. Lightly hydrolyzed whey tastes similar to regular whey, while heavily hydrolyzed whey can taste noticeably bitter.

Because the protein is already partly broken down, it can be absorbed somewhat faster. In a 2009 study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, older men given 35 g of hydrolyzed casein had faster protein digestion and absorption and 25 to 50% higher blood amino acid levels than those given intact casein. Muscle protein synthesis tended to be higher with the hydrolysate, but the difference was not statistically significant.

For healthy adults, there is little evidence that the faster absorption of hydrolysate leads to more muscle over time than regular whey isolate or concentrate. The ISSN position stand groups hydrolysates and isolates together as the most researched whey forms around exercise. Whole whey is already a fast-digesting protein, so the extra speed may not matter much for most people.

Hydrolysates are also used in infant formulas and medical nutrition because smaller peptides can be less likely to trigger some milk allergy reactions, though a hydrolysate is not safe for everyone with a milk allergy. In sports products, hydrolysate usually raises the price. It may help if you find regular whey hard on your stomach, but it is not needed for good results.
onLabel: Listed as "hydrolyzed whey protein," "whey protein hydrolysate" or "hydrolyzed whey protein isolate." Many products include only a small amount, so check where it falls in the ingredient order.

short: Micellar casein is the slow-digesting main protein of milk, kept in its natural clustered form, and it is often taken before bed to supply amino acids overnight.
body: Casein makes up about 80% of the protein in cow's milk, and whey makes up the other 20%. In milk, casein exists in tiny clusters called micelles. Micellar casein is made by filtering skim milk to concentrate these micelles while removing most of the lactose, fat and whey, without the acid treatment used for older casein forms such as caseinates.

The main feature of casein is how slowly it digests. In the acidic stomach, casein forms a gel or clot that empties gradually, so amino acids enter your blood over several hours. Whey, by contrast, is digested quickly and causes a faster, shorter spike. This difference is why casein is often marketed as a nighttime protein.

The research supports a modest benefit. In a 2012 study in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise, 16 young men who took 40 g of casein 30 minutes before sleep after evening exercise had better overnight whole-body protein balance than with a placebo. Muscle protein synthesis was about 22% higher, a result that was borderline significant. The ISSN position stand on protein says 30 to 40 g of casein before sleep can increase overnight muscle protein synthesis and metabolic rate. Whether this leads to more muscle than eating the same total protein at other times is still debated.

Casein is a high-quality, complete protein that is rich in essential amino acids. It mixes thicker than whey and works well in puddings and baking. Because it comes from milk, it is not suitable if you have a milk allergy, though it is usually low in lactose.
onLabel: Listed as "micellar casein" or "micellar casein isolate." Ingredients such as "calcium caseinate" or "sodium caseinate" are related but processed differently.

short: Milk protein isolate is a dairy protein made by filtering skim milk, keeping both casein and whey in milk's natural ratio of about 80 to 20.
body: Milk protein isolate (MPI) is made by passing skim milk through fine filters that hold back the protein while letting much of the water, lactose and minerals pass through. Unlike whey or casein products, MPI keeps both milk proteins together in roughly the same proportions as milk, about 80% casein and 20% whey. Products usually reach around 85 to 90% protein by weight. A closely related ingredient, milk protein concentrate (MPC), contains a bit less protein and more lactose.

Because it contains both proteins, MPI digests at a medium pace. The whey part is absorbed fairly quickly while the casein part releases amino acids more slowly. That blend makes MPI common in ready-to-drink shakes, meal replacements and protein bars, where it also adds a creamy texture and holds up well during heat processing.

Milk proteins rank among the highest-quality proteins. In a 2017 pig study in the British Journal of Nutrition, milk protein concentrate scored 100 or more on DIAAS, the top category. The ISSN position stand on protein notes that milk proteins, which combine whey and casein, have been well studied for supporting muscle gains alongside resistance training.

MPI is usually cheaper than whey isolate. It is lower in lactose than milk but generally has more than whey isolate, so sensitive people may still notice symptoms. Like all dairy proteins, it is not suitable for anyone with a milk allergy. If you want one protein for both daytime shakes and a slower-digesting option, MPI is a practical middle choice.
onLabel: Listed as "milk protein isolate," "milk protein concentrate" or "MPI/MPC." It is often the first ingredient in ready-to-drink protein shakes.

short: Pea protein isolate is a plant protein extracted from yellow split peas, typically about 80 to 90% protein, and is the most common base for vegan protein powders.
body: Pea protein isolate is made from dried yellow split peas. The peas are milled into flour, mixed with water, and the protein is separated from the starch and fiber, then dried. Most commercial pea protein is around 80 to 90% protein by weight. It is free of dairy, soy and gluten, which makes it popular for people avoiding common allergens.

Pea protein is relatively high in lysine and the branched-chain amino acids but low in methionine, which is its limiting amino acid. That is why pea is often blended with rice protein, which has the opposite pattern. Pea protein usually scores well on PDCAAS but below the top quality tier on DIAAS. In a 2017 pig study, pea protein concentrate scored below 75, the cut-off for a "good" protein claim.

Research on muscle gain is encouraging but limited. In a 2015 trial in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, 161 young men training for 12 weeks took pea protein, whey or a placebo. Across the whole group the differences were not significant, while in the weakest participants pea produced more muscle thickness gain than placebo, and whey did not differ from either. The study was partly funded by a pea protein maker. Larger servings can help make up for lower leucine.

Heavy metals are worth watching. In Consumer Reports' 2025 testing of 23 protein powders and shakes, plant-based products averaged about nine times more lead than dairy-based ones, and all the plant products tested were made from peas. Choosing brands that publish independent heavy metal results is a sensible step.
onLabel: Listed as "pea protein isolate" or "pea protein." In blends, pea is often paired with "brown rice protein" to balance the amino acid profile.

short: Soy protein isolate is a plant protein made from defatted soybeans that contains about 90% protein and provides all nine essential amino acids in useful amounts.
body: Soy protein isolate is made from soybeans that have had their oil removed. The remaining soy flakes are processed to separate the protein from carbohydrates and fiber, giving a powder that is about 90% protein on a dry basis. It has been used in foods for decades and is one of the most studied plant proteins.

Soy is a complete protein. It scores 1.0 on PDCAAS, the top score, and lands in the "good" range of 75 to 99 on the stricter DIAAS scale in some studies. It has less leucine than whey per gram, but a slightly larger serving can close that gap.

For building muscle, soy compares well with animal proteins. A 2018 meta-analysis in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism pooled nine studies with 266 people and found no significant difference in strength or lean mass gains between soy and animal proteins such as whey or beef during resistance training.

Soy contains isoflavones, plant compounds that are structurally similar to estrogen. This has caused concern among some buyers, but research in men generally does not show meaningful effects on testosterone or estrogen at normal intakes. Isolate usually has fewer isoflavones than whole soy foods, though amounts vary by processing. Soy is one of the major food allergens, so it must be declared on U.S. labels and is not suitable for people with a soy allergy. Soy isolate is often among the least expensive protein sources per gram.
onLabel: Listed as "soy protein isolate" or "isolated soy protein," and declared under the allergen statement as "Contains: Soy."

short: Brown rice protein is a plant protein extracted from whole-grain brown rice, usually about 80% protein, and often blended with pea protein to balance its amino acids.
body: Brown rice protein is made by treating brown rice with enzymes that break down the starch, then separating and drying the protein. Most powders reach about 75 to 90% protein by weight. It is free of dairy, soy and gluten, and has a mild, slightly earthy taste and a gritty texture compared with whey.

Rice protein's limiting amino acid is lysine, which is lower than in most other proteins. Pea protein is high in lysine but low in methionine, while rice is the reverse. That is why so many vegan powders combine the two, often in a ratio near 70% pea to 30% rice. A blend can score higher on protein quality measures than either protein alone.

For muscle building, one study is often cited. In a 2013 trial in Nutrition Journal, 24 resistance-trained men took 48 g of rice protein isolate or whey protein isolate after training for eight weeks. Both groups gained lean mass and strength and lost fat, with no significant difference between groups. The dose was large, the study was short, and there was no non-supplemented group, so the results do not prove rice and whey are equal at smaller servings.

Rice plants absorb arsenic and other metals from soil and water more readily than many crops, so heavy metals are a fair question for rice-based powders. Federal limits for heavy metals in supplements do not exist, so look for brands that share independent lab results for lead, arsenic and cadmium per serving.
onLabel: Listed as "brown rice protein" or "organic brown rice protein." In blends it usually appears after pea protein.

short: Hemp protein is a plant protein powder made by grinding pressed hemp seeds, typically containing about 30 to 50% protein along with fiber and fat.
body: Hemp protein is made from the seeds of the hemp plant (Cannabis sativa). The seeds are pressed to remove most of the oil, and the remaining seed cake is milled and sifted into powder. Unlike pea or soy isolate, hemp protein is usually not highly refined, so it keeps more fiber, healthy fats and minerals. Most hemp powders contain about 30 to 50% protein by weight, so a serving gives less protein per scoop than an isolate.

Hemp's limiting amino acid is lysine. A 2010 study in the Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry measured PDCAAS for 30 hemp products and found values similar to or higher than some grains, nuts and pulses. Removing the hull improved digestibility. Reported scores for whole hemp seed products were roughly 0.5, with dehulled seed reaching about 0.6 or more, well below whey or soy.

Hemp seed products sold as food contain only trace amounts of THC, the compound in cannabis that causes a high. In the U.S., hemp is defined as cannabis with no more than 0.3% THC on a dry-weight basis. Athletes in drug-tested sports should still check their organization's rules, since some governing bodies restrict hemp products.

Hemp protein suits people who want a whole-food, minimally processed plant powder and value the fiber, which is often 5 g or more per serving. If your main goal is high protein per scoop or a high leucine dose, an isolate or a pea and rice blend will deliver more protein for the same calories.
onLabel: Listed as "hemp protein," "hemp seed protein" or "hemp protein powder." Check the grams of protein per serving, since it is often lower than for isolates.

short: Collagen peptides are collagen protein broken into short chains by enzymes so they dissolve easily, but collagen lacks tryptophan and is an incomplete protein.
body: Collagen is the main structural protein in skin, tendons, ligaments and bone. Collagen peptides, also called hydrolyzed collagen, are made by heating animal hides, bones or fish skin to extract gelatin, then using enzymes to cut it into small peptides. The result dissolves in hot or cold liquids with little taste.

Collagen has an unusual amino acid makeup. It is very high in glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, but it contains essentially no tryptophan, an essential amino acid. That makes it an incomplete protein with a PDCAAS of 0. It is also low in leucine compared with whey or soy.

For muscle building, collagen does not match complete proteins. In a 2020 study in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, healthy older women took 30 g of whey or collagen peptides twice a day. Whey produced larger increases in muscle protein synthesis over both a few hours and a full week. If your goal is muscle, collagen should not be your main protein source.

Collagen is studied for other uses, such as joint pain, skin and tendon health, often at doses of about 10 to 15 g per day. Some results are positive, but many studies are small or industry funded, so the evidence is mixed. Collagen still counts toward the grams of protein printed on the label, because labels measure protein by nitrogen content. That can make a collagen-heavy blend look like a better protein source than it is.
onLabel: Listed as "collagen peptides," "hydrolyzed collagen" or "bovine/marine collagen." When collagen is blended into a protein powder, it adds to the grams of protein even though it is incomplete.

short: Egg white protein is a powder made by drying pasteurized egg whites, providing a complete, dairy-free protein with about 80% protein by weight.
body: Egg white protein powder is made by separating egg whites from the yolks, pasteurizing them to kill bacteria such as Salmonella, and spray-drying the liquid into powder. The main protein in egg white is ovalbumin, and the powder is often sold as "egg white albumin." Most powders are about 80% protein by weight, with almost no fat and no lactose.

Egg protein has long been a reference point for protein quality. It is a complete protein with all nine essential amino acids in good proportions and scores at the top of PDCAAS. Egg was one of the proteins evaluated in the FAO's 2013 protein quality report. It digests at a moderate pace, slower than whey but faster than casein.

Research on egg protein powders for muscle building is thinner than for whey, but the ISSN position stand on protein lists egg among the high-quality protein sources for athletes. A 25 g serving provides roughly 2 g of leucine, a bit less than whey.

Egg white protein is a good option if you avoid dairy but still want an animal protein. It is naturally free of lactose and gluten. It is not suitable if you are allergic to eggs, which is one of the most common food allergies in children. Egg white powder can taste slightly sulfurous and mixes thinner than whey. It is often more expensive per gram than whey concentrate.
onLabel: Listed as "egg white protein," "egg albumin" or "dried egg whites," with an allergen statement such as "Contains: Egg."

short: Beef protein isolate is a dairy-free protein powder made by breaking down beef tissue into a concentrated, hydrolyzed protein, often high in collagen-type amino acids.
body: Beef protein isolate is made by cooking beef tissue in water, then using enzymes to break the protein into smaller pieces and filtering and drying the result. Products are typically 90% or more protein by weight and contain little fat or carbohydrate. It is marketed as a dairy-free animal protein for people who cannot tolerate whey.

The amino acid profile depends heavily on what part of the animal is used. Many beef protein isolates are made largely from connective tissue rather than lean muscle. That tissue is rich in collagen, so the product can be high in glycine and proline and lower in leucine and other essential amino acids than you might expect from "beef." Some brands add free amino acids to improve the profile. Check the amino acid table if one is provided.

Research is limited. In a 2018 study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 41 adults doing eight weeks of resistance training took beef protein isolate, hydrolyzed chicken protein or whey concentrate after workouts. All three protein groups gained lean mass compared with baseline and there were no differences in strength between groups, but the study was small.

Beef protein isolate is free of dairy, lactose, soy and eggs, so it can suit people with several food allergies. In Consumer Reports' 2025 testing, beef-based powders had lower lead levels than plant-based ones on average but higher than dairy. It often costs more per gram than whey.
onLabel: Listed as "beef protein isolate" or "hydrolyzed beef protein." If the label shows a high glycine and proline content, a large share is likely collagen.

short: Bone broth protein is a powder made by simmering animal bones and connective tissue, then drying the broth, so most of its protein is collagen.
body: Bone broth is made by simmering bones, joints and connective tissue in water for many hours. Bone broth protein powder takes that broth and concentrates and dries it into a powder. Because the starting material is mostly bone and connective tissue, most of the protein is collagen and gelatin rather than the muscle proteins found in meat.

That means bone broth protein shares collagen's limits. It is high in glycine, proline and hydroxyproline, low in leucine, and very low in tryptophan, an essential amino acid. As a result, it is not a complete protein and is not a strong choice for building muscle compared with whey, casein, egg or soy.

Bone broth is often promoted for joints, skin and gut health, but the evidence is limited. A 2019 study in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism measured key collagen-building amino acids in bone broths. Broths had lower levels than the collagen supplements used in research, commercial broths had less than homemade ones, and amounts varied widely between recipes. The authors concluded that bone broth is unlikely to be a reliable source of these amino acids.

Bone broth protein powders can still be useful as a savory, dairy-free way to add some protein to soups or drinks. Since the protein grams on the label are measured by nitrogen content, they count collagen the same as complete protein. Compare the price per gram and the amino acid profile before you buy.
onLabel: Listed as "bone broth protein" or "chicken/beef bone broth concentrate." Labels may also list collagen content separately, which can make up most of the protein.

American Journal of Clinical Nutrition (Oikawa et al., whey vs collagen peptides), 2020

short: Amino spiking is the practice of adding cheap free amino acids or other nitrogen-rich ingredients to a protein powder so its listed protein content looks higher.
body: Amino spiking, also called protein spiking, happens when a manufacturer adds inexpensive amino acids such as glycine or taurine, or other nitrogen-rich ingredients such as creatine, to a protein powder. These ingredients raise the total protein figure on the label without adding much useful, complete protein.

It works because of how protein is measured. Under U.S. labeling rules in 21 CFR 101.9, protein content may be calculated by measuring the nitrogen in a food and multiplying it by 6.25. That method assumes all the nitrogen comes from protein. Free amino acids and some non-protein compounds also contain nitrogen, so they can inflate the number. A powder claiming 25 g of protein might contain noticeably less real whey.

Amino spiking drew wide attention in the mid-2010s, when several supplement companies faced class-action lawsuits over spiked protein claims. Many brands now advertise themselves as "no amino spiking" and publish full amino acid profiles. Glycine itself is not harmful, and taurine and creatine have their own uses. The problem is paying for protein you are not getting.

You can look for warning signs. Check the ingredient list for free amino acids such as glycine, taurine, L-glutamine, L-arginine or creatine near a protein blend. Compare the total protein to the amino acid profile if one is given: an unusually high glycine figure or low leucine for the stated protein is a red flag. Independent lab testing that measures the actual amino acid content is the most reliable check.
onLabel: Look for free amino acids such as "glycine," "taurine" or "L-glutamine" listed in or near the protein blend, especially inside a proprietary blend.

sources.name: U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 101.9 Nutrition Labeling of Food (LII)

short: A proprietary blend is a group of ingredients listed under one name with a combined total weight, without disclosing how much of each ingredient it contains.
body: A proprietary blend is a mix of ingredients that a company lists under a single name, such as "Protein Matrix" or "Anabolic Blend." For dietary supplements, U.S. rules in 21 CFR 101.36 allow this. The label must show the total weight of the blend and list its ingredients in descending order of weight, but it does not have to say how much of each ingredient is inside.

Companies say blends protect their formulas from copycats. The downside for you is that you cannot tell the exact amounts. A protein blend that lists "whey protein isolate, whey protein concentrate, soy protein isolate" might be mostly the cheapest ingredient, even if isolate is named first by a small margin. In pre-workout and fat-burner products, blends can also hide low doses of featured ingredients.

Proprietary blends are one way amino spiking can be hidden. Free amino acids such as glycine or taurine can sit inside a blend labeled as protein, adding to the stated grams without being complete protein.

Not every blend is a problem, and many protein powders sold as conventional foods simply list ingredients in order without any blend name. Still, full disclosure makes it easier to judge value. If a product uses a proprietary blend, look for an amino acid profile, third-party testing, or a brand that lists each ingredient's amount. When two products cost the same, the one that shows you exactly what is inside is easier to trust.
onLabel: On a Supplement Facts panel, the blend name appears with a single total weight and its ingredients listed below it in descending order, with no individual amounts.

sources.name: U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 101.36 Nutrition Labeling of Dietary Supplements (LII)

short: Protein density is the share of a protein powder's serving weight that is actually protein, calculated by dividing grams of protein by the serving size in grams.
body: Protein density tells you how much of each scoop is protein and how much is everything else. To calculate it, divide the grams of protein per serving by the serving size in grams, then multiply by 100. For example, a 32 g scoop with 25 g of protein is about 78% protein by weight. A 45 g scoop with 25 g of protein is only about 56%.

The rest of the scoop is made up of other ingredients: carbohydrates, fat, flavorings, cocoa, sweeteners, thickeners such as xanthan gum, added vitamins, creamers and moisture. Some of these improve taste and texture. But a lower protein density means you are paying for more non-protein material and usually taking in more calories per gram of protein.

Typical ranges depend on the protein type. Unflavored whey isolate often reaches 85 to 90% protein by weight. Flavored whey isolate is often around 75 to 85%, whey concentrate around 65 to 80%, and plant blends around 65 to 80%. Hemp powders, mass gainers and meal replacement shakes are much lower, sometimes under 50%, because they are designed to include carbohydrates, fat or fiber.

Protein density is a quick way to compare products, but it does not measure protein quality. A collagen-heavy or amino-spiked powder can look dense on paper. Use it alongside the protein source, the amino acid profile and the cost per 25 g of protein to get a fuller picture.
onLabel: Not printed directly on labels. Calculate it from the Nutrition or Supplement Facts panel: grams of protein divided by the serving size in grams.

sources.name: U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 101.9 Nutrition Labeling of Food (LII)
U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Serving Size on the Nutrition Facts Label, 2024

short: Cost per 25 g of protein is a value measure that shows how much you pay for 25 grams of actual protein, letting you compare products with different scoop sizes.
body: Protein powders come in many tub sizes, scoop sizes and protein levels, so the sticker price or price per serving can mislead. Cost per 25 g of protein puts every product on the same footing by asking one question: how much does it cost to get 25 grams of protein from this product? We use 25 g because it is a common serving size and falls within the 20 to 40 g per-meal range suggested by the ISSN position stand on protein.

Here is the math. First, find the total protein in the container: grams of protein per serving times servings per container. Then divide the price by that total and multiply by 25. For example, a $50 tub with 30 servings of 24 g of protein holds 720 g of protein. $50 divided by 720 g, times 25, equals about $1.74 per 25 g of protein.

This measure often changes the ranking. A tub with a low price per serving might use small 18 g protein scoops, while a pricier tub might deliver 27 g per scoop. Larger containers and subscription discounts usually lower the cost, and flavored products often cost slightly more per gram of protein than unflavored ones.

Cost per 25 g does not account for protein quality or contamination. A powder with collagen or added free amino acids can look cheap per gram while giving you less useful protein. Pair this number with the protein source, protein density and any third-party testing before deciding.
onLabel: Not printed on labels. Calculate it from the price, the servings per container and the grams of protein per serving on the Nutrition or Supplement Facts panel.

sources.name: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, ISSN Position Stand: Protein and Exercise, 2017
U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Serving Size on the Nutrition Facts Label, 2024

short: Serving size is the amount of a product that the label's nutrition numbers describe, such as one 30 g scoop. It is not a recommendation.
body: The serving size is the amount the Nutrition Facts or Supplement Facts panel is based on. Every number on the panel, including calories, protein and sugar, applies to that one serving. The FDA says serving sizes reflect the amounts people typically eat or drink and are not a recommendation for how much you should consume.

For conventional foods, serving sizes are set using FDA reference amounts customarily consumed, listed in 21 CFR 101.12. For dietary supplements, the serving size is expressed in a unit that fits the product form, such as scoops or packets. Protein powders can be sold under either set of rules, which is why you will see both Nutrition Facts and Supplement Facts panels in the same aisle.

On protein powders, the serving size usually appears as both a scoop count and a weight in grams, such as "1 scoop (31 g)." The gram weight is the number to trust. Scoops vary in size between brands and are often not packed the same way you would fill them at home, and powder settles during shipping.

Serving size matters for comparisons. Two products may both claim 25 g of protein, but if one needs a 31 g scoop and the other a 40 g scoop, the second contains more non-protein ingredients. Divide protein grams by the serving weight to get protein density, and use servings per container to calculate cost per 25 g of protein. If you use two scoops, double every number on the label.
onLabel: Shown at the top of the Nutrition Facts or Supplement Facts panel as a scoop count with grams, along with servings per container.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Serving Size on the Nutrition Facts Label, 2024
U.S. Code of Federal Regulations, 21 CFR 101.12 Reference Amounts Customarily Consumed (LII)

short: Sucralose is a zero-calorie artificial sweetener made from sugar that is about 600 times sweeter than table sugar and is widely used in flavored protein powders.
body: Sucralose is a high-intensity sweetener made by chemically modifying sucrose (table sugar), replacing three of its hydrogen-oxygen groups with chlorine atoms. The FDA approved it as a general-purpose sweetener in 1999. It is about 600 times sweeter than sugar, so only tiny amounts are needed, often well under 100 mg per scoop of protein powder. Most of it passes through the body without being absorbed, which is why it adds essentially no calories.

The FDA set an acceptable daily intake (ADI) for sucralose of 5 mg per kg of body weight per day. For a 70 kg (154 lb) adult, that is 350 mg per day, which is far more than most people get from food and drinks. Sucralose is heat stable, so it is also used in baking and in heat-treated ready-to-drink shakes.

Research on its longer-term effects is mixed. Some studies suggest sucralose may affect gut bacteria or blood sugar responses in some people, while others find no meaningful effect. In 2023, a laboratory study in the Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health found that sucralose-6-acetate, an impurity and breakdown product of sucralose, damaged DNA in cell tests. Those were test-tube findings, not human studies, and regulators have not changed their safety conclusions in response.

If you prefer to avoid sucralose, many brands offer unflavored versions or use stevia or monk fruit instead. Sucralose is often paired with acesulfame potassium, because the two together taste more like sugar.
onLabel: Listed as "sucralose" in the ingredients, usually near the end because very little is used. It is sometimes known by the brand name Splenda.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food, 2025
Journal of Toxicology and Environmental Health, Part B (Schiffman et al., sucralose-6-acetate), 2023

short: Acesulfame potassium, or Ace-K, is a zero-calorie artificial sweetener about 200 times sweeter than sugar, often combined with sucralose in flavored protein powders.
body: Acesulfame potassium, often shortened to Ace-K or acesulfame K, is a synthetic high-intensity sweetener. It is about 200 times sweeter than table sugar, so only small amounts are needed. Your body does not break it down for energy, and it is excreted unchanged, which is why it adds no calories.

The FDA approved Ace-K for specific uses in 1988 and as a general-purpose sweetener in 2003. The agency has set an acceptable daily intake (ADI) of 15 mg per kg of body weight per day. For a 70 kg (154 lb) adult, that is 1,050 mg per day, far more than the amount in a scoop or two of protein powder.

Ace-K is rarely used alone. On its own it can leave a slightly bitter aftertaste, so manufacturers pair it with other sweeteners such as sucralose or aspartame. The blend tastes more like sugar and allows lower amounts of each sweetener. Ace-K is also heat stable, which makes it suitable for baked goods and heat-processed ready-to-drink shakes.

Major regulators consider Ace-K safe at normal intakes. Like other artificial sweeteners, it has been the subject of studies on gut bacteria, appetite and metabolic health, with mixed and mostly short-term results. Evidence in humans has not shown clear harm at typical intakes. If you would rather avoid artificial sweeteners, look for unflavored powders or ones sweetened with stevia or monk fruit, and check the full ingredient list since sweeteners are often combined.
onLabel: Listed as "acesulfame potassium," "acesulfame K" or "Ace-K," usually near the end of the ingredients and often next to sucralose.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food, 2025

short: Stevia is a zero-calorie sweetener made from purified compounds called steviol glycosides, extracted from the leaves of the Stevia rebaudiana plant and 200 to 400 times sweeter than sugar.
body: Stevia sweeteners come from the leaves of Stevia rebaudiana, a plant native to South America. The sweet taste comes from compounds called steviol glycosides, such as rebaudioside A (Reb A), rebaudioside M (Reb M) and stevioside. According to the FDA, these are reported to be 200 to 400 times sweeter than table sugar, and they provide essentially no calories.

The FDA treats purified and crude stevia differently. It has not questioned the generally recognized as safe (GRAS) status of high-purity steviol glycosides, meaning extracts that are at least 95% pure. Whole stevia leaves and crude stevia extracts are not considered GRAS for use as sweeteners, and their import for that purpose is not permitted. So the stevia in your protein powder is a highly refined extract, not ground leaves.

Stevia is popular in products marketed as natural or clean label. Its main drawback is taste: some steviol glycosides, especially Reb A, can leave a bitter or licorice-like aftertaste at higher levels. Newer extracts such as Reb M taste closer to sugar but cost more. Many brands blend stevia with monk fruit, erythritol or natural flavors to smooth the flavor.

Research on stevia's effects on blood sugar, appetite and gut bacteria is still developing and results are mixed, but regulators consider purified steviol glycosides safe at normal intakes. If you dislike its aftertaste, try a product sweetened another way or an unflavored powder you can sweeten yourself.
onLabel: Listed as "stevia leaf extract," "steviol glycosides," "Reb A" or "Reb M," usually near the end of the ingredients.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food, 2025

short: Monk fruit extract is a zero-calorie sweetener made from the Luo Han Guo fruit, whose sweet compounds called mogrosides are 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar.
body: Monk fruit, also called Luo Han Guo (Siraitia grosvenorii), is a small round fruit grown in southern China. Its sweetness comes mainly from compounds called mogrosides, especially mogroside V. Extracts made from the fruit are reported by the FDA to be 100 to 250 times sweeter than table sugar, and they provide essentially no calories in the small amounts used.

The FDA has not questioned GRAS (generally recognized as safe) notices for monk fruit extract as a sweetener, and no acceptable daily intake (ADI) has been specified. That usually means regulators did not see a safety concern at expected levels of use.

Monk fruit is popular in protein powders marketed as natural or keto-friendly. On its own it can have a fruity or slightly lingering aftertaste and is expensive, so it is often blended with other sweeteners. A common pairing is monk fruit plus erythritol, a sugar alcohol, which adds bulk and a more sugar-like taste. That matters if you are sensitive to sugar alcohols, since the product may contain more erythritol than monk fruit.

Human research specifically on monk fruit is limited compared with older sweeteners. Most evidence comes from regulatory safety reviews and lab studies on mogrosides. As with stevia, the "natural" label describes where the sweetener comes from, not whether it is healthier than other approved sweeteners. If you choose monk fruit products, check the full ingredient list to see what it is blended with.
onLabel: Listed as "monk fruit extract," "Luo Han Guo extract" or "Siraitia grosvenorii fruit extract," often next to erythritol or stevia.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food, 2025

short: Sugar alcohols are low-calorie sweeteners such as erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and maltitol that taste sweet but are only partly absorbed, so they can cause digestive upset.
body: Sugar alcohols, also called polyols, are carbohydrates with a structure that is part sugar and part alcohol, though they contain no ethanol. Common examples are erythritol, xylitol, sorbitol and maltitol. According to the FDA, they range from about 25% to 100% as sweet as sugar, are slightly lower in calories, do not promote tooth decay and do not cause a sudden rise in blood sugar.

In protein powders, sugar alcohols add sweetness and bulk, and they are often paired with high-intensity sweeteners such as stevia or monk fruit. Erythritol is the most common in powders because most of it is absorbed and passed out in urine, so it is less likely to cause gut symptoms than others.

Because the body does not fully absorb most sugar alcohols, larger amounts can cause gas, bloating or a laxative effect. Tolerance differs from person to person, and sorbitol and maltitol tend to cause more trouble than erythritol. Xylitol is very toxic to dogs, so keep products with it away from pets.

Research on erythritol has raised questions. A 2023 study in Nature Medicine found that higher blood erythritol levels were linked to a greater risk of heart attack and stroke in people already at risk, and erythritol made platelets clot more easily in lab tests. The human findings were observational and cannot prove cause, but the authors called for more long-term safety studies. If you have heart disease risk factors, it may be reasonable to talk with your doctor.
onLabel: May appear as a "Sugar Alcohol" line under carbohydrates on the Nutrition Facts panel, which is optional unless a sugar claim is made, and by name, such as "erythritol," in the ingredients.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Aspartame and Other Sweeteners in Food, 2025
Nature Medicine (Witkowski et al., erythritol and cardiovascular event risk), 2023

short: Xanthan gum is a thickener made by fermenting sugar with bacteria, added to protein powders in small amounts to give shakes a smoother, thicker texture.
body: Xanthan gum is a type of soluble fiber made when the bacterium Xanthomonas campestris ferments sugars. The resulting gum is purified, dried and ground into a powder. Even tiny amounts thicken liquids, so it is used in salad dressings, sauces, gluten-free baking and many protein powders. In the EU it is labeled as E 415.

In a protein shake, xanthan gum helps the powder stay suspended, reduces separation and gives a creamier, thicker feel in the mouth. Amounts are small, typically well under 1 gram per serving, so it adds almost no calories. It also helps cover the thin, watery texture of some isolates and plant proteins.

Regulators consider xanthan gum safe. In a 2017 re-evaluation, the European Food Safety Authority concluded that there was no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake and no safety concern for the general population at the reported uses. Like other fibers, larger doses, generally several grams or more per day, can cause gas, bloating or looser stools. A later EFSA review in 2023 looked at its use in special foods for very young infants.

Xanthan gum is often listed with other gums such as guar gum, gum acacia or cellulose gum. If you are very sensitive to fibers or follow a low-FODMAP style diet for digestive symptoms, you may want to note how many gums a product contains. For most people, the small amount in a protein shake is not a concern.
onLabel: Listed as "xanthan gum," usually near the end of the ingredients, often alongside other gums such as "guar gum" or "cellulose gum."

sources.name: EFSA Journal, Re-evaluation of xanthan gum (E 415) as a food additive, 2017

short: Carrageenan is a thickener and stabilizer extracted from red seaweed, used mainly in ready-to-drink protein shakes and dairy products to keep them smooth and prevent separation.
body: Carrageenan is a family of carbohydrates extracted from certain red seaweeds. It is used as a thickener, gelling agent and stabilizer, especially in dairy drinks, where it reacts with milk proteins to keep the drink smooth and stop ingredients from settling. In the EU it is labeled as E 407. You are more likely to find it in ready-to-drink protein shakes than in dry powders.

Carrageenan has a controversial reputation. Some animal and cell studies suggested it might promote gut inflammation, and a related substance called degraded carrageenan, or poligeenan, is a possible carcinogen. Poligeenan is not approved as a food additive. Regulators view food-grade carrageenan as a different substance, but some critics argue that part of it could break down in the gut.

The most detailed recent review came from the European Food Safety Authority in 2018. It kept a temporary group acceptable daily intake of 75 mg per kg of body weight per day, which is far above typical intake from food. However, EFSA called the safety data incomplete, flagged uncertainties and asked for better data within five years. So the evidence is mixed: no clear harm at normal intakes in humans, but open questions.

If you have inflammatory bowel disease or find that carrageenan products upset your stomach, it is reasonable to avoid it, and many brands now market carrageenan-free shakes. This is general information, so talk with your doctor if you have a specific digestive condition.
onLabel: Listed as "carrageenan" in the ingredients, usually near the end. It appears more often in ready-to-drink shakes than in powders.

sources.name: EFSA Journal, Re-evaluation of carrageenan (E 407) and processed Eucheuma seaweed (E 407a), 2018

short: Digestive enzymes in protein powders are added proteins, such as proteases or lactase, that are meant to help break down protein or lactose during digestion.
body: Your body already makes enzymes that break down food: proteases for protein, amylases for starch, lipases for fat and lactase for milk sugar. Some protein powders add extra enzymes, often from plants or fungi. Common ones include proteases such as bromelain (from pineapple) and papain (from papaya), and lactase. Many are sold under trademarked names as blends.

Brands claim these enzymes help you absorb more protein or reduce bloating. The evidence is limited. A 2008 study in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition gave healthy men whey protein concentrate with or without a protease blend and found higher blood amino acid levels over four hours with the enzymes. However, the study was small, open label and tested a commercial enzyme product, and few independent studies have followed. Higher blood amino acids in the short term have not been shown to mean more muscle.

Lactase has a clearer role. It breaks down lactose into simpler sugars, so adding it to a whey concentrate may help people with lactose intolerance tolerate the product better. If you have trouble with dairy, though, switching to whey isolate or a non-dairy protein may work more reliably.

Enzymes are generally considered safe in the small amounts used. People with allergies to pineapple, papaya or certain molds should check the source. For most healthy people, the body digests whey, casein, egg and soy well without help, so added enzymes are an optional extra rather than a must-have.
onLabel: Often listed as an "enzyme blend" with names such as "protease," "bromelain," "papain" or "lactase," sometimes with activity units instead of milligrams.

sources.name: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition (Oben et al., protease enzymes with whey), 2008
NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, Definition & Facts for Lactose Intolerance (accessed 2026)

short: Lactose is the natural sugar in milk, and the amount left in a dairy protein powder depends on processing, with whey concentrate containing more than whey isolate.
body: Lactose is a sugar found naturally in milk and dairy products. To digest it, your small intestine uses an enzyme called lactase to split lactose into glucose and galactose. Many people make less lactase after childhood. When lactose is not fully broken down, bacteria in the colon ferment it, which can cause gas, bloating, cramps or diarrhea.

Lactose malabsorption is very common. According to the NIH's National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, about 68% of the world's population has it, and about 36% of people in the United States. It is most common in people of African and Asian descent. Only people who get symptoms are considered lactose intolerant, and most can still handle some lactose.

In protein powders, lactose levels depend on how much the dairy protein is filtered. Whey protein concentrate keeps more lactose, often a few grams per serving. Whey protein isolate is filtered further and usually has less than 1 g per serving. Milk protein isolate and micellar casein fall in between. Hydrolysates do not necessarily remove lactose. Some products add lactase enzyme to help.

If dairy proteins bother you, try a whey isolate first, since many lactose-intolerant people tolerate it well. If you still have symptoms, egg, beef or plant proteins avoid lactose entirely. Lactose intolerance is not the same as a milk allergy, which is an immune reaction to milk proteins; people with a milk allergy need to avoid dairy proteins altogether.
onLabel: Usually not listed by name. Look at total sugars on the panel for a rough estimate, since in unsweetened dairy powders most sugar is lactose, and check for "lactase" in the ingredients.

sources.name: NIH National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, Definition & Facts for Lactose Intolerance (accessed 2026)

short: Grass-fed whey is whey protein made from the milk of cows that eat mostly grass or forage, though there is no single U.S. federal standard for the dairy claim.
body: Grass-fed whey comes from milk produced by cows raised mainly on pasture or forage such as grass and hay, rather than a diet with large amounts of grain. Many grass-fed whey products come from Ireland or New Zealand, where pasture grazing is common for much of the year.

The term is not tightly defined for dairy in the United States. The USDA withdrew its voluntary grass-fed marketing standard in 2016, so there is no single federal rule for what share of a cow's diet must be grass for its milk to be labeled grass-fed. Some brands use third-party certifications, such as programs from grassfed associations, that set clearer rules on diet and pasture access. Without a certification, the claim relies on the brand's own sourcing standards.

Grass-fed milk does differ in some ways. A 2018 study in Food Science & Nutrition analyzing more than 1,100 milk samples found that milk from cows fed nearly all forage had more omega-3 fats and a lower omega-6 to omega-3 ratio than conventional milk. Several authors worked for an organic dairy cooperative. More importantly for protein powder, these differences are in the milk fat, and whey protein, especially isolate, contains very little fat. The protein itself, including its amino acid profile, is essentially the same.
Choosing grass-fed whey is mainly about animal welfare, farming practices or personal values. It is not likely to change your muscle-building results, and it usually costs more per gram of protein.
onLabel: Appears as a front-label claim such as "grass-fed" or "pasture-raised," sometimes with a certification seal. The ingredient list usually just says "whey protein."

sources.name: Food Science & Nutrition (Benbrook et al., grass-fed milk fatty acids), 2018

short: Cold processed is a marketing term for whey made with low-temperature filtering methods, meant to limit protein denaturation, but it has no regulatory definition.
body: "Cold processed" usually means a whey protein was separated using low-temperature filtering methods such as microfiltration or ultrafiltration, rather than methods that use more heat or strong pH changes. The goal is to keep more of the whey proteins in their native, unfolded state, along with smaller fractions such as lactoferrin and immunoglobulins.

The term has no official definition. No U.S. regulation sets a temperature limit or test for a cold-processed claim, so one brand's cold processing may not match another's. All whey also has to be pasteurized for safety, which involves heat, and the powder is spray-dried. What the label usually describes is the filtering step that happens after pasteurization.

Processing can affect protein structure. A 2021 study in the International Dairy Journal tracked whey protein changes through each step of making native whey powder by microfiltration and found denaturation was minimal throughout, while heat steps and processing type made a difference for specific proteins. Gentle processing can preserve more native protein.

Whether that matters for you is less clear. When you eat any protein, stomach acid and enzymes unfold and break it down anyway, so denatured whey still supplies the same amino acids for building muscle. There is little evidence that cold processing improves muscle growth. It may matter more for specific bioactive fractions, but the effects at protein-shake doses are not well established. Treat cold processed as a manufacturing detail, not a reason to pay much more.
onLabel: Appears as a front-label claim such as "cold processed," "cold filtered" or "cross-flow microfiltered." It does not appear in the ingredient list or nutrition panel.

sources.name: International Dairy Journal (Muuronen et al., processing effects on whey proteins), 2021

short: Prop 65 is a California law requiring a warning when a product can expose you to a listed chemical, such as lead, above a set safe harbor level.
body: Proposition 65, officially the Safe Drinking Water and Toxic Enforcement Act of 1986, is a California law approved by voters in 1986. It requires the state to keep a list of chemicals known to cause cancer, birth defects or other reproductive harm. The list is maintained by California's Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA), is updated at least once a year, and includes several hundred chemicals.

Businesses that sell products in California must give a clear warning if a product can expose people to a listed chemical above a set level, unless they can show the exposure is below the "safe harbor" threshold. Lead is the chemical that most often triggers warnings on protein powders. Its safe harbor level for reproductive harm is 0.5 micrograms per day, a strict limit that Consumer Reports also used as its level of concern in its 2025 protein powder testing.

A Prop 65 warning is a right-to-know notice, not a ruling that a product is unsafe or illegal. It tells you a listed chemical is present above the threshold, not how far above. Because the limits are strict and lawsuits are common, some companies add warnings as a precaution even when exposure may be low. Other companies simply do not sell in California.
For protein powders, a warning is a signal to look further. Ask the brand for its heavy metal test results per serving, check for independent testing, and consider how many servings you use each day.
onLabel: Shown as a "WARNING" statement on the package, product page or shelf, usually naming a chemical such as lead and linking to www.P65Warnings.ca.gov.

sources.name: California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment (OEHHA), Proposition 65 (accessed 2026)
Consumer Reports, Protein Powders and Shakes Contain High Levels of Lead, 2025

short: Heavy metals in protein powders are trace contaminants such as lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury that come mostly from the soil and water where ingredients are grown.
body: In food testing, "heavy metals" usually means four toxic elements: lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury. They occur naturally in the earth's crust and are also spread by human activity such as mining and industry. The FDA notes that plants take up trace amounts from the soil and water where they are grown, and organic crops absorb them just as conventional crops do. Over time, high exposure can harm the brain, kidneys and other organs, and lead is especially concerning for children and during pregnancy.

Protein powders can contain these metals because their ingredients come from plants or animals. Plant proteins such as pea and rice tend to carry more, and chocolate flavors can add more because cacao often contains lead and cadmium. In Consumer Reports' 2025 testing of 23 protein powders and shakes, more than two-thirds had more lead per serving than CR's daily level of concern of 0.5 micrograms. Plant-based products averaged about nine times more lead than dairy-based ones.

Experts disagree on how worried to be. A 2020 risk assessment in Toxicology Reports, using earlier test data, concluded that typical use of protein powders was unlikely to cause harm from heavy metals. Critics argue that small exposures add up across your whole diet, and there are no federal limits on heavy metals in supplements.

To lower your exposure, choose brands that publish independent heavy metal results per serving, favor dairy or egg proteins if you use powders daily, limit servings to what you need, and rotate products.
onLabel: Heavy metals are not listed on Nutrition or Supplement Facts panels. You may see a Prop 65 warning, a certification seal, or a link to a brand's lab test results.

short: Informed Choice is a third-party certification program that tests sports nutrition products on store shelves for substances banned in sport and checks how they are made.
body: Informed Choice is a quality assurance program for supplements and sports nutrition products, run by the same organization as Informed Sport. Brands pay to join, and products that meet the standards can display the Informed Choice logo. The program is aimed at everyday active people and recreational athletes who want some assurance that a product is not contaminated with banned substances.

According to the program, Informed Choice combines monthly testing of products bought from retail shelves with third-party oversight of the manufacturing facilities and processes. The testing focuses on substances banned in sport, such as stimulants and anabolic agents, which can end up in supplements by accident through shared equipment or contaminated ingredients, or on purpose.

Informed Choice is different from Informed Sport. Informed Sport tests every single batch before it is released for sale, which gives athletes stronger assurance about the specific product they buy. Informed Choice relies on ongoing sampling rather than testing every batch, so it is designed more for general consumers than for drug-tested athletes.

A certification like this does not mean a product works, tastes good or is low in heavy metals. It also does not confirm the full label content, such as exact protein grams, unless the program says so. It is mainly a check for banned substances and manufacturing quality. You can confirm a product's status by searching the Informed Choice website rather than relying only on the logo.
onLabel: Shown as the Informed Choice logo on the package or product page. You can search the product on the program's website to confirm it is currently certified.

short: Informed Sport is a third-party certification program that tests every batch of a product for substances banned in sport before it is released for sale.
body: Informed Sport is a banned-substance testing program for sports supplements, run by the same organization as Informed Choice. It was built for elite athletes and other people who face drug testing, such as military personnel, who could lose their careers if a supplement turns out to contain a prohibited substance.

The key feature is batch testing. According to the program, Informed Sport tests every single batch of a certified product before it is released to market, screening for a long list of substances banned in sport, over 300 compounds by the program's count. Manufacturing sites are also reviewed. Each tested batch can be looked up on the Informed Sport website, so you can check the batch number on your container against the results.

Contamination is a real concern in sports supplements. Stimulants, steroids or other banned substances can get into products through shared factory equipment, contaminated raw materials or deliberate adulteration. Under anti-doping rules, athletes are usually responsible for anything found in their bodies, so testing helps lower, though not remove, that risk.

Informed Sport certification is about banned substances. It does not prove a product works, verify every nutrition claim, or test for heavy metals unless stated. No program can promise zero risk, since only samples from each batch are tested. If you compete in a drug-tested sport, Informed Sport and NSF Certified for Sport are the two programs most often recommended.
onLabel: Shown as the Informed Sport logo on the label. Look up your container's batch number on the Informed Sport website to confirm that batch was tested.

short: NSF Certified for Sport is a supplement certification that screens products for substances banned in sport, confirms label contents and audits manufacturing facilities.
body: NSF Certified for Sport is a certification program run by NSF, an independent public health and safety organization. It was designed to help athletes reduce the risk of a positive drug test from contaminated supplements. According to NSF, the program is recognized by the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency (USADA), Major League Baseball, the National Hockey League and the Canadian Football League, and several other leagues and organizations recommend it.

Certification has several parts. NSF says products are tested for close to 300 substances banned in sport, based on lists such as the World Anti-Doping Agency's. NSF also confirms that what is on the label is in the product, screens for contaminants such as heavy metals, reviews the formula and label, and inspects production facilities and suppliers. Certified products are tested on a lot-by-lot basis and monitored over time.

Compared with some other seals, NSF Certified for Sport covers more than banned substances, because it also checks label claims and contaminants. That makes it one of the most comprehensive certifications for protein powders and other sports supplements.

Even so, certification does not mean a product will improve your performance or that it is right for you. It also cannot remove all risk, since testing uses samples. Some sports organizations restrict hemp or CBD products even when certified, so check your own organization's rules. Confirm a product's status in NSF's online listing or app instead of relying on a logo, since counterfeit or outdated seals do appear.
onLabel: Shown as the NSF Certified for Sport mark on the label. Search the product or lot in NSF's online listing or app to verify it.

NSF Certified for Sport, program home page (accessed 2026)

short: Clean Label Project is an organization that tests consumer products, including protein powders, for contaminants such as heavy metals, pesticides and plasticizers, and certifies products that meet its standards.
body: Clean Label Project (CLP) is a U.S. organization that tests food and consumer products for contaminants that do not appear on labels. It focuses on heavy metals such as lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury, pesticide residues, and plasticizers such as BPA and phthalates. Products that pass its testing can display a Clean Label Project Certified seal, and the group also gives separate awards and publishes reports.

CLP drew wide attention for protein powders in 2018, when it published test results on more than 130 products and reported measurable heavy metals in most of them, with plant-based powders generally showing more lead than whey. Its data were later used by other researchers, including a 2020 risk assessment in Toxicology Reports.

CLP certification is different from sports certifications such as NSF Certified for Sport or Informed Sport. Those focus mainly on substances banned in sport. CLP focuses on environmental and industrial contaminants. The two types answer different questions, and a product may carry one, both or neither.

There are limits to keep in mind. Brands typically pay to be certified, and CLP sets its own thresholds, which are not government limits. A seal shows that a product met CLP's standards in testing, not that it has zero contaminants. CLP certification also does not check protein content or effectiveness. To confirm a product's status, check Clean Label Project's website rather than relying only on the package.
onLabel: Shown as a Clean Label Project Certified seal or award logo on the package. Verify the product on Clean Label Project's website.

short: Third-party testing means an independent lab or certification group, not the brand itself, checks a product for what it contains, contaminants or banned substances.
body: In the United States, dietary supplements, including many protein powders, are not approved by the FDA before they are sold. The FDA says it is not authorized to approve supplements for safety and effectiveness before marketing. Companies are responsible for making safe products with accurate labels, and the FDA mainly acts after problems appear. Third-party testing fills part of that gap.

Third-party testing comes in several forms. Certification programs such as NSF Certified for Sport and Informed Sport focus on substances banned in sport, and NSF also checks label claims and contaminants. Programs such as Clean Label Project focus on heavy metals, pesticides and plasticizers. Some brands also send samples to independent labs and publish a certificate of analysis (COA) showing results for protein content, amino acids, heavy metals or microbes.

Each type answers a different question. A banned-substance seal does not tell you about lead, and a heavy metal certificate does not tell you about banned stimulants. A COA is only useful if it comes from an accredited lab, matches your product's batch or lot number, and is recent. Testing also does not prove a product works.

When you compare protein powders, look for the specific type of testing that matches your concerns. If you are a drug-tested athlete, choose a sport certification. If you use protein daily, look for published heavy metal results per serving. Always confirm a seal on the certifier's own website, since logos can be outdated or copied.
onLabel: Shown as certification seals on the package, or as a QR code, batch lookup or link to a certificate of analysis on the brand's website.

short: Muscle protein synthesis is the process your body uses to build new muscle proteins, driven mainly by eating protein and doing resistance exercise.
body: Your muscles are always being rebuilt. Muscle protein synthesis (MPS) is the building side, where amino acids are linked together into new muscle proteins. Muscle protein breakdown is the other side. When synthesis is higher than breakdown over time, you gain muscle; when breakdown wins, you lose it. Scientists usually measure MPS in the lab using amino acids tagged with stable isotopes.

Two things raise MPS the most: eating protein and doing resistance exercise, and the effects add up when you combine them. Essential amino acids, especially leucine, trigger the rise. The ISSN position stand on protein suggests 20 to 40 g of high-quality protein, or about 0.25 g per kg of body weight, per meal, with doses spread every three to four hours. About 10 g of essential amino acids is enough to maximize MPS in many people.

The response depends on the person and situation. Older adults often need more protein per meal for the same response, a pattern sometimes called anabolic resistance. After very intense, full-body training, some studies found 40 g raised MPS more than 20 g.

MPS is a short-term measure, and it does not always predict long-term muscle gain. What matters most over months is total daily protein and consistent training. A 2018 meta-analysis in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found that protein supplements helped resistance-training gains in muscle mass and strength, with benefits leveling off around 1.6 g of protein per kg of body weight per day, though the true cut-off could be higher.
