short: Protein timing is the idea that when you eat protein around a workout affects muscle gains, often described as a short post-workout "anabolic window."
body: The anabolic window is the popular belief that you must drink a protein shake within 30 to 60 minutes after training or you will miss your chance to build muscle. The idea came from studies showing that muscle is especially responsive to protein after resistance exercise. Protein timing more broadly also covers how you spread protein through the day and whether to eat it before bed.

Later research made the window look much wider. A 2013 meta-analysis in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition found that once total daily protein was taken into account, protein timing had no significant effect on muscle size or strength. Total protein intake was the strongest predictor. The ISSN position stand on nutrient timing notes that muscle stays more sensitive to protein for about 24 hours after a workout.

Timing still has some role. The ISSN suggests eating 20 to 40 g of high-quality protein every three to four hours and having protein within about two hours after training, which is easy to do with normal meals. If you train fasted first thing in the morning, eating protein sooner afterward makes more sense. A 30 to 40 g serving of casein before sleep may also support overnight muscle protein synthesis, though long-term benefits are less certain.

For most people, the practical order of priorities is total daily protein first, then spreading it across three to five meals, then fine-tuning timing around training. If drinking a shake right after training helps you hit your daily target, it is a fine habit. Missing that 30-minute mark is not a reason to worry.

short: Nitrogen balance is the difference between the nitrogen you take in from protein and the nitrogen you lose, used to estimate whether your body is gaining or losing protein.
body: Protein is the main source of nitrogen in your diet. On average, protein is about 16% nitrogen by weight, which is why labs multiply nitrogen by 6.25 to estimate protein. Nitrogen balance compares the nitrogen you eat with the nitrogen you lose, mostly in urine, plus smaller amounts in stool, sweat and skin.

If you take in more nitrogen than you lose, you are in positive nitrogen balance, which happens during growth, pregnancy, recovery from illness, or muscle gain. If you lose more than you take in, you are in negative balance, which can happen with low protein or calorie intake, serious illness or injury. When intake and losses match, you are in balance, as most healthy adults are when weight is stable.

Nitrogen balance studies are the main basis for the U.S. Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for protein. The National Academies used them to find the protein intake at which healthy adults stop losing body nitrogen, then added a safety margin to set the RDA at 0.8 g per kg of body weight per day.

The method has known limits. It is hard to collect every nitrogen loss, and errors tend to make intake look more adequate than it is, so some researchers believe nitrogen balance underestimates protein needs. It also measures the whole body, not muscle specifically. Newer methods, such as the indicator amino acid oxidation technique, have suggested somewhat higher needs. That is one reason sports nutrition groups recommend more protein than the RDA for active people.
onLabel: Not shown on labels, but the protein grams on a label are usually calculated from nitrogen content multiplied by 6.25, the same conversion used in nitrogen balance studies.

short: The RDA for protein is 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day for healthy adults, the amount set to meet the needs of nearly all healthy people.
body: The Recommended Dietary Allowance (RDA) for protein comes from the National Academies' Dietary Reference Intakes, published in 2005. For healthy adults it is 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight per day. That works out to about 56 g per day for a 70 kg (154 lb) person and about 46 g for a 57 kg (126 lb) person. The RDA is set high enough to cover the needs of about 97 to 98% of healthy people.

The RDA is based mainly on nitrogen balance studies. The average requirement was set at 0.66 g per kg per day, and a safety margin was added to reach 0.8 g. The same report gives an acceptable range of 10 to 35% of daily calories from protein for adults.

The RDA is a minimum to prevent deficiency, not an ideal target for everyone. The ISSN position stand on protein recommends 1.4 to 2.0 g per kg per day for most people who exercise. A 2018 meta-analysis found benefits for muscle gain with resistance training leveled off around 1.6 g per kg per day, though some people may benefit from up to about 2.2 g. For adults over 65, the PROT-AGE study group recommends at least 1.0 to 1.2 g per kg per day, and more during illness.
Needs vary with age, activity, health and calorie intake. People with kidney disease may need to limit protein, so check with your doctor. This is general information, not personal medical advice.
onLabel: Labels use a different benchmark: the FDA Daily Value for protein is 50 g per day for adults and children 4 and older, based on a 2,000-calorie diet.

short: Sarcopenia is the age-related loss of muscle strength and muscle mass that can make daily tasks harder and raise the risk of falls, frailty and disability.
body: Sarcopenia is a muscle disease that becomes more common with age. Muscle mass and strength start to decline gradually from middle age, and the loss speeds up in older adults, especially with inactivity, illness or poor nutrition. Sarcopenia is linked to falls, fractures, loss of independence and higher health care needs.

The European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP2) updated its definition in 2019. It puts low muscle strength first. Low strength makes sarcopenia probable, low muscle quantity or quality confirms it, and poor physical performance, such as slow walking speed, marks it as severe. Suggested grip strength cut-offs are under 27 kg for men and under 16 kg for women, measured with a handheld dynamometer.

Resistance exercise is the most effective way to slow or reverse muscle loss, and protein supports it. Older muscles respond less to a given dose of protein, a pattern called anabolic resistance, so older adults may need more protein per meal. The PROT-AGE study group recommends at least 1.0 to 1.2 g of protein per kg of body weight per day for adults over 65, 1.2 g or more for those who are active, and 1.2 to 1.5 g for many with acute or chronic illness. People with severe kidney disease may need less.

Protein powders can be a convenient way for older adults to reach those targets, especially when appetite is small. Whey and other high-leucine proteins are well studied. If you are concerned about muscle loss, talk with your doctor, as this is general information rather than medical advice.

Journal of the American Medical Directors Association (PROT-AGE Study Group), 2013

short: Clear whey is a whey protein isolate processed and acidified so it mixes into a thin, see-through, juice-like drink instead of a milky shake.
body: Clear whey, sometimes sold as clear whey isolate or protein water, is a whey protein isolate that has been further processed and made acidic. When mixed with water, it forms a thin, transparent drink that tastes more like juice or a sports drink than a milkshake. It is usually sold in fruit flavors.

Acidity is the key. Whey proteins stay clear and dissolve well at low pH. A 2010 study in the Journal of Food Science found that whey protein drinks at pH 3.6 and below stayed clear both before and after heat treatment, while at higher pH the choice of ingredients mattered much more. Clear whey powders often include acids such as citric acid and may use defoaming agents to reduce foam when shaken.

Nutritionally, clear whey is still whey isolate. It provides complete protein, is rich in leucine and is usually low in lactose, fat and carbohydrate. A typical serving supplies about 20 g of protein. Because extra processing is involved, it usually costs more per gram of protein than standard whey isolate, so check the cost per 25 g of protein.

Clear whey suits people who dislike thick shakes, want something refreshing after training in hot weather, or feel bloated by creamy drinks. Its acidity is similar to fruit juice or soda, so if you drink it often, rinsing your mouth with water afterward may help protect tooth enamel. Let it settle after shaking, since foam is common.
onLabel: Usually listed as "whey protein isolate" or "hydrolyzed whey protein isolate" followed by acids such as "citric acid" and sometimes an "anti-foaming agent."

Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition, ISSN Position Stand: Protein and Exercise, 2017

short: A mass gainer is a high-calorie powder that combines protein with large amounts of carbohydrate and often fat, designed to help people who struggle to eat enough to gain weight.
body: A mass gainer, or weight gainer, is a powder made to add a large number of calories in one shake. Servings often provide 600 to 1,250 calories, with roughly 25 to 60 g of protein and 100 to 250 g of carbohydrate, usually from maltodextrin, oat flour or other starches, plus some fat. Serving sizes are large, often 150 to 330 g of powder.

Gaining muscle requires enough calories, not just enough protein. A 2019 review in the journal Sports on off-season nutrition for bodybuilders suggested a modest calorie surplus of about 10 to 20% above maintenance, aiming to gain about 0.25 to 0.5% of body weight per week for newer lifters, with protein of 1.6 to 2.2 g per kg per day. A larger surplus tends to add more fat without much extra muscle.

Mass gainers can help if you have a small appetite, a very high calorie need, or limited time to eat. But you can build a similar shake from regular protein powder, milk, oats, banana and nut butter, often for less money and with more fiber. Many gainers have low protein density and plenty of added sugar.

Because servings are so large, contaminants per serving can add up. In Consumer Reports' 2025 testing, the product with the highest lead per serving was a plant-based mass gainer. If you use a gainer daily, look for published heavy metal results and consider whether half a serving meets your needs. Compare cost per 25 g of protein against a regular protein powder.
onLabel: Labels show large serving sizes, often several scoops or 150 g or more, with high calories and carbohydrates. The first ingredient is often maltodextrin rather than a protein.

Consumer Reports, Protein Powders and Shakes Contain High Levels of Lead, 2025

short: A meal replacement shake is a drink designed to stand in for a meal, providing protein plus carbohydrate, fat, fiber and added vitamins and minerals in a measured calorie amount.
body: A meal replacement shake is meant to replace a whole meal, not just add protein. A typical serving provides about 200 to 400 calories, with 15 to 30 g of protein, along with carbohydrates, some fat, fiber and a mix of vitamins and minerals. They come as powders or ready-to-drink bottles.

A protein powder, by contrast, is mostly protein with few other nutrients. Drinking a basic protein shake in place of meals day after day can leave gaps in fiber, healthy fats and micronutrients. In the United States there is no specific federal standard for what a product labeled meal replacement must contain, so formulas vary widely. Compare the full nutrition panel, not just the protein number.

Meal replacements are best studied for weight loss. A 2003 meta-analysis in the International Journal of Obesity pooled six studies and found that people using partial meal replacement plans, usually replacing one or two meals a day, lost about 2.4 to 2.5 kg more weight at three months and one year than people on standard reduced-calorie diets. The structure and fixed calorie count make portion control easier.

Meal replacements are convenient, but whole meals usually offer more fiber, variety and fullness. They work best as a tool for busy days or a weight-loss plan rather than a full diet. If you have diabetes, kidney disease or other health conditions, or are using shakes as your main source of nutrition, talk with your doctor or a registered dietitian first.
onLabel: Labels usually show a fuller nutrition panel with fiber, fat and a long list of added vitamins and minerals with percent Daily Values. Some are labeled as dietary supplements and others as foods.

U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Serving Size on the Nutrition Facts Label, 2024

short: Ready-to-drink protein shakes are pre-mixed, shelf-stable or refrigerated bottles or cartons, typically providing 20 to 42 g of protein with no mixing required.
body: Ready-to-drink (RTD) protein shakes are pre-made drinks sold in bottles, cartons or cans. Most are shelf stable because they are heat-treated using ultra-high-temperature (UHT) or retort processing and sealed in sterile packaging. Common protein sources are milk protein concentrate or isolate, whey, and pea or soy for plant versions. Protein content usually ranges from about 20 to 42 g per container.

Because the drink has to stay smooth and stable for months, RTDs often contain more additives than powders. Stabilizers and thickeners such as carrageenan, gellan gum or cellulose gum keep protein from settling, and emulsifiers help mix in fats. Sweeteners such as sucralose and acesulfame potassium are common. Heat processing is easier with milk proteins and casein, which is why many RTDs use them.

The main tradeoff is cost and convenience. RTDs are easy to carry and need no shaker, which can help you hit a protein target on busy days. But they often cost noticeably more per gram of protein than powder, sometimes two or three times as much. Calculate cost per 25 g of protein using the price per bottle.

Quality and contaminants still matter. Consumer Reports' 2025 testing included ready-to-drink shakes alongside powders, and some had lead above its level of concern. The protein quality depends on the source used, so check whether it is milk, whey or plant based. If you drink one every day, look for published testing and keep an eye on total sweetener and additive intake.
onLabel: The Nutrition Facts panel covers one bottle or carton. Protein sources such as "milk protein concentrate" usually lead the ingredients, followed by stabilizers such as "carrageenan" or "gellan gum."
